canonical_statement: The study sought to longitudinally examine the availability and non-prescribed use of buprenorphine-naloxone among people who use drugs in Vancouver, Canada.

Data came from two ongoing open prospective Vancouver cohorts: VIDUS, enrolling HIV-negative people who had injected drugs within the prior month, and ACCESS, enrolling HIV-positive people who had used an unregulated substance other than cannabis within the prior month.

population.label: VIDUS and ACCESS prospective cohorts in Vancouver

canonical_statement: For this analysis, participants had to report a history of injection drug use and complete at least one study visit between December 2014 and March 2020.

population.label: Analytic sample
inclusion_criteria: At least one study visit between December 2014 and March 2020

canonical_statement: Participants completed interviewer-administered questionnaires at cohort entry and semi-annually thereafter covering demographics, drug-use patterns and behaviours, and interactions with healthcare and criminal-justice systems.
Immediate availability of non-prescribed BUP-NX was defined as self-reported ability to acquire it within less than 10 minutes.

outcome.definition: Self-reported ability to acquire non-prescribed BUP-NX within less than 10 minutes at the time of interview.

canonical_statement: Delayed availability of non-prescribed BUP-NX was defined as self-reported ability to acquire it, but taking longer than 10 minutes.

outcome.definition: Self-reported ability to acquire non-prescribed BUP-NX, but taking longer than 10 minutes.

canonical_statement: No availability of non-prescribed BUP-NX was defined as reporting that the participant could not obtain it.

outcome.definition: Self-reported inability to obtain non-prescribed BUP-NX (could not score).

canonical_statement: Non-prescribed BUP-NX use was defined as past-6-month self-reported use when the drug was not prescribed or was taken for the experience or feeling it caused.

outcome.definition: Self-reported use of BUP-NX when it was not prescribed or taken for the experience/feeling it caused during the prior 6 months.

canonical_statement: Calendar year of interview was the primary explanatory variable; additional candidate variables covered demographics, housing/neighbourhood, drug-use intensity, opioid agonist therapy, overdose, treatment access, naloxone possession, incarceration, and drug dealing.

Baseline characteristics were compared by immediate versus no immediate BUP-NX availability using Pearson chi-squared tests for categorical variables and Mann-Whitney U tests for continuous variables.
Trends in non-prescribed BUP-NX availability over time were analyzed using the Cochrane-Armitage test for trend.

Bivariable and multivariable generalized estimating equation logistic regression models were used for immediate and delayed availability versus no availability; variables associated at p<0.10 in bivariable analyses entered multivariable models, and analyses used two-sided p-values in SAS 9.4.
The analytic sample included 1,617 participants; 966 (60%) were male and 914 (58%) were of white ethnicity, with a median baseline age of 47 years (IQR 37-54).

canonical_statement: Because the study was observational, causal interpretations of the reported associations cannot be made.
The outcomes relied on self-report of sensitive information, so response bias could not be excluded.

Generalizability to all people who use drugs in Vancouver or to other Canadian or US jurisdictions is uncertain, particularly given local fentanyl exposure and broad access to multiple opioid agonist therapies.
The study could not determine the underlying drivers of the observed availability trends from these data alone; the authors suggested qualitative follow-up research.
The authors concluded that reported non-prescribed BUP-NX availability increased markedly from 2014 to 2020 without a corresponding increase in reported non-prescribed use.
The authors argued that concerns about relaxing BUP-NX prescribing restrictions may be overstated and that such restrictions may unnecessarily impede access to treatment.
